ety.text: From Middle English plot, plotte, from late Old English plot (“a plot of ground”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Proto-Germanic *plataz, *platjaz (“a patch”); or alternatively, perhaps from a rebracketing of Old English land-splott (“small portion, or plot, of ground”) taken as landes-plot (“plot of land”). Compare Middle Low German plet (“patch, strip of cloth, rags”), German Bletz (“rags, bits, strip of land”), and possibly Gothic 𐍀𐌻𐌰𐍄 (plat, “a patch, rags”). See also plat. See also complot for an influence and reinforcement of noun sense 8.

senses.d: The course of a story, comprising a series of incidents which are gradually unfolded, sometimes by unexpected means.
An area or land used for building on or planting on.

ex: He's buried in the family plot.

senses.d: A ground plan, map; a nautical chart.
A sketch or outline detailing the arrangement of something; a plan.
A synopsis of a literary work.
A graph or diagram drawn by hand or produced by a mechanical or electronic device.
ex: I was told to fly out on a vector of 100 degrees to meet a strong plot of aircraft 30 miles from the coast.

senses.d: A secret plan to achieve an end, the end or means usually being illegal or otherwise questionable.
ex: The plot would have enabled them to get a majority on the board.
The assassination of Lincoln was part of a larger plot.

senses.d: Contrivance; deep reach thought; ability to plot or intrigue.
Participation in any stratagem or conspiracy.
ex: And when Christ saith, Who marries the divorced commits adultery, it is to be understood, if he had any plot in the divorce.
They were plotting against the king.

senses.d: To trace out (a graph or diagram).
ex: They plotted the number of edits per day.

senses.d: To mark (a point on a graph, chart, etc).
ex: Every five minutes they plotted their position.
This treatise plotteth down Cornwall as it now standeth.
